danish.title: Femtende bog (1812–13) — Kapitel 12
paragraphs: Som det almindeligvis sker, mærkede Pierre ikke de fulde virkninger af de fysiske savn og anstrengelser, han havde lidt som fange, før de var overstået. Efter sin befrielse nåede han Orjol, og på tredje dagen dér, da han forberedte sig på at rejse til Kiev, blev han syg og lå tre måneder. Han havde, hvad lægerne kaldte »galdefeber«. Men trods det faktum, at lægerne behandlede ham, årelod ham og gav ham medicin at drikke, kom han sig.

Næsten intet indtryk sad tilbage i Pierres sind af alt, hvad der var sket fra hans redning til hans sygdom. Han huskede kun det ensformigt grå vejr, snart regnfuldt, snart snebelagt, indre fysisk ubehag, smerter i fødder og side. Han huskede et generelt indtryk af andres ulykker og lidelser og af at blive plaget af nysgerrigheden hos officerer og generaler, der udspurgte ham; han huskede også besværet med at skaffe et køretøj og heste og frem for alt sin manglende evne til at tænke og føle i hele den tid. Den dag, han blev reddet, havde han set liget af Petja Rostov. Samme dag erfarede han, at fyrst Andrej, der havde overlevet Borodino-slaget i over en måned, for nylig var død i familien Rostovs hus i Jaroslavl, og Denisov, der fortalte ham denne nyhed, nævnte også Hélènes død, i formodning om at Pierre længe havde vidst det. Alt dette virkede i øjeblikket blot underligt på Pierre: han følte, at han ikke kunne begribe betydningen. Alt han brændte efter var at komme bort så hurtigt som muligt fra steder, hvor folk dræbte hinanden, til et fredeligt tilflugtssted, hvor han kunne komme sig, hvile og tænke over alle de mærkelige nye ting, han havde erfaret; men da han nåede Orjol, blev han straks syg. Da han kom til sig selv efter sin sygdom, så han to af sine tjenere, Terenti og Vaska, der var kommet fra Moskva, samt sin kusine, den ældste fyrstinde, der havde boet på hans gods ved Jelets og var kommet for at passe ham, da hun hørte om hans redning og sygdom.

Det var først gradvist under sin rekonvalescens, at Pierre tabte de indtryk, han havde vænnet sig til i de foregående måneder, og vænnet sig til tanken om, at ingen ville tvinge ham til at gå nogetsteds hen i morgen, at ingen ville fratage ham hans varme seng, og at han med sikkerhed ville få sin middag, te og aftensmad. Men længe endnu drømte han sig stadig tilbage i fangenskabets kår. På samme måde begyndte han lidt efter lidt at forstå de nyheder, han havde fået fortalt efter sin redning — om fyrst Andrejs død, hans kones død og franskmændenes tilintetgørelse.

En glad følelse af frihed — den fuldstændige, umistelige frihed, der er mennesket naturlig, og som han første gang havde oplevet ved det første holdt uden for Moskva — fyldte Pierres sjæl under hans rekonvalescens. Han var overrasket over at opdage, at denne indre frihed, som var uafhængig af ydre omstændigheder, nu ligesom havde fået en ekstra ramme af ydre frihed. Han var alene i en fremmed by uden bekendte. Ingen krævede noget af ham og sendte ham nogetsteds hen. Han havde alt, hvad han behøvede: tanken om hans kone, der havde været en vedvarende pine for ham, var der ikke længere, for hun var ikke mere.

»Å, hvor er det godt! Hvor vidunderligt!« sagde han til sig selv, når et pænt dækket bord med duftende bouillon blev skubbet hen til ham, eller når han lagde sig om natten i en blød, ren seng, eller når han huskede, at franskmændene var borte, og at hans kone ikke levede mere. »Å, hvor godt, hvor vidunderligt!«
Og af gammel vane stillede han sig spørgsmålet: »Nå, og hvad så? Hvad skal jeg tage mig til?« Og han gav sig straks selv svaret: »Nå, jeg skal leve. Ak, hvor herligt!«

Selve det spørgsmål, der førhen havde plaget ham — det, han hele tiden havde søgt at finde svar på — livets mål — eksisterede ikke længere for ham. Jagten på livets mål var ikke blot midlertidigt forsvundet — han følte, at den ikke længere fandtes for ham og ikke kunne melde sig igen. Og netop dette fravær af et mål gav ham den fuldstændige, glade følelse af frihed, der udgjorde hans lykke på denne tid.

Han kunne ikke se noget mål, for nu havde han tro — ikke tro på nogen slags regel, ord eller idéer, men tro på en evigt levende, evigt nærværende Gud. Før havde han søgt Ham i de mål, han satte sig. Den jagt efter et mål havde ganske enkelt været en jagt efter Gud, og pludselig havde han i sit fangenskab lært — ikke af ord eller ræsonnementer, men af en direkte følelse — hvad hans barnepige havde fortalt ham for længe siden: at Gud er her og overalt. I sit fangenskab havde han lært, at i Karatajev (Platon Karatajev) var Gud større, mere uendelig og ufattelig end i frimurernes Universets Arkitekt. Han følte sig som en mand, der efter at have anstrengt øjnene for at se ud i det fjerne opdager det, han søgte, lige for sine fødder. Hele sit liv havde han set hen over hovederne på mennesker omkring sig, når han blot burde have set lige frem for sig uden at anstrenge øjnene.

Før havde han aldrig kunnet finde det store, uudgrundelige, uendelige noget. Han havde blot følt, at det måtte findes et sted, og havde ledt efter det. I alt nært og forståeligt havde han kun set det begrænsede, smålige, almindelige og meningsløse. Han havde udstyret sig med en mental kikkert og set ud i det fjerne, hvor den smålige verdsligdom, der gemte sig i diset afstand, havde forekommet ham stor og uendelig, blot fordi den ikke var tydeligt synlig. Og sådan havde det europæiske liv, politik, frimureri, filosofi og filantropi forekommet ham. Men selv dengang, i de øjeblikke af svaghed, som han plejede at kalde dem, var hans sind trængt ud i de fjerne egne, og også dér havde han set den samme smålighed, verdsligdom og meningsløshed. Nu havde han imidlertid lært at se det store, evige og uendelige i alt, og derfor — for at se det og nyde dets betragtning — kastede han med glæde den kikkert, han hidtil havde stirret henover menneskers hoveder med, og så med fryd det evigtforanderlige, evigt store, uudgrundelige og uendelige liv omkring sig. Og jo nærmere han så, desto mere rolig og lykkelig blev han. Det forfærdelige spørgsmål »Hvad for?« som før havde ødelagt alle hans mentale bygningsværker, eksisterede ikke længere for ham. Til det spørgsmål — »Hvad for?« — var et enkelt svar nu altid parat i hans sjæl: »Fordi der er en Gud, den Gud, uden hvis vilje ikke et hår falder fra et menneskes hoved.«

english.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: As generally happens, Pierre did not feel the full effects of the physical privation and strain he had endured as a prisoner until after they were over. After his liberation, he reached Orel, and on the third day there, when preparing to continue to Kiev, he fell ill and was bedridden for three months. He had what the doctors called "bilious fever." But despite the fact that they treated him, bled him, and gave him medicine, he recovered.

Very little impression was left on Pierre's mind by everything that happened from his rescue to his illness. He remembered only the dull gray weather, now rainy and now snowy, internal physical distress, and pains in his feet and side. He recalled a general impression of people's misfortunes and suffering, of being pestered by the curiosity of officers and generals who questioned him, and the difficulty of finding a carriage and horses. Above all, he remembered his inability to think and feel during that time. On the day of his rescue, he had seen Petya Rostov's body. That same day, he learned that Prince Andrew, after surviving the battle of Borodino by more than a month, had recently died at the Rostovs' house in Yaroslavl, and Denisov, who told him this, also mentioned Helene's death, assuming Pierre had heard about it long ago. All of this seemed merely strange to Pierre at the time—he felt unable to grasp its significance. Just then, his only desire was to get away as quickly as possible from places where people were killing one another, to some peaceful refuge where he could recover, rest, and make sense of all the strange new things he had learned. But upon reaching Orel, he immediately fell ill. When he came to after his illness, he saw two of his servants attending him—Terenty and Vaska, who had come from Moscow—as well as his cousin the eldest princess, who had been living on his estate at Yelets and, hearing of his rescue and illness, had come to look after him.

It was only gradually during his recovery that Pierre shed the impressions he had grown accustomed to over the past months and got used to the idea that no one would force him to go anywhere tomorrow, that no one would take away his warm bed, and that he would certainly get his dinner, tea, and supper. But for a long time he still dreamed of captivity. In the same gradual way, he came to absorb the news he had been told after his rescue: the death of Prince Andrew, the death of his wife, and the destruction of the French.

A joyous feeling of freedom—that complete, innate freedom natural to every person, which he had first experienced at the initial halt outside Moscow—filled Pierre's soul during his recovery. He was surprised to find that this inner freedom, which was independent of external circumstances, now came with the added bonus of external liberty. He was alone in a strange town, without acquaintances. No one demanded anything of him or sent him anywhere. He had everything he wanted; the thought of his wife, which had been a constant torment, was gone now that she was no more.

"Oh, how wonderful! How splendid!" he said to himself when a neatly set table was brought to him with savory broth, or when he lay down at night in a soft, clean bed, or when he remembered that the French were gone and his wife was no more. "Oh, how wonderful, how splendid!"
And from old habit he asked himself: "Well, and what next? What am I going to do?" And he immediately gave himself the answer: "Well, I shall live. Ah, how splendid!"

The very question that had formerly tormented him, the thing he had endlessly sought—the aim of life—no longer existed for him now. That search for an aim hadn't merely disappeared temporarily; he felt it no longer existed and could never arise again. And this very absence of any aim gave him the complete, joyous sense of freedom that constituted his happiness at this time.

He could not see an aim, for he now had faith—not faith in any kind of rule, or words, or ideas, but faith in an ever-living, ever-present God. Before, he had sought God through the aims he set himself. That search for an aim had been simply a search for God. And suddenly, in captivity, he had learned—not through words or reasoning but through direct feeling—what his old nurse had told him long ago: that God is here and everywhere. In captivity he had learned that in Karataev, God was greater, more infinite and unfathomable, than in the Architect of the Universe recognized by the Freemasons. He felt like a man who, after straining his eyes to see into the far distance, discovers what he sought right at his feet. All his life he had looked over the heads of the people around him, when he should have simply looked straight ahead without straining his eyes.

In the past he had never been able to find that great, inscrutable, infinite something. He had only felt that it must exist somewhere and had searched for it. In everything near and understandable, he had seen only what was limited, petty, ordinary, and meaningless. He had equipped himself with a mental telescope and peered into the distance, where the petty everyday world, hidden in mist, had seemed great and infinite simply because it wasn't clearly visible. European life, politics, Freemasonry, philosophy, philanthropy—all had seemed that way. But even then, in moments of what he had considered weakness, his mind had penetrated those distances and seen the same pettiness, worldliness, and meaninglessness there too. Now, however, he had learned to see the great, the eternal, and the infinite in everything, and so—to see it and take joy in contemplating it—he naturally threw away the telescope through which he had been gazing over people's heads, and gladly beheld the ever-changing, eternally great, unfathomable, and infinite life around him. And the closer he looked, the more at peace and happy he became. That terrible question "What for?"—which had once demolished all his mental constructions—no longer existed for him. To that question, "What for?" a simple answer now always stood ready in his soul: "Because there is a God, that God without whose will not a single hair falls from a man's head."
